summary.text: The zodiac is a belt of sky extending about 8° north and south of the ecliptic, the Sun's apparent path across the celestial sphere over the year.
It is divided into 12 equal signs of 30° each, which roughly correspond to the constellations Aries through Pisces.
The system originated in Babylonian astronomy in the 1st millennium BC, and today the names of the signs are mostly associated with horoscopic astrology.

items.prompt: The word zodiac comes from a Greek word relating to little animals. What does the name reflect?

options.label: The tiny size of the stars in each sign
The prominence of animals among the twelve signs
The animals that farmers kept in each month
The pets of the astronomers who named it

items.explain: The name reflects the prominence of animals, and mythological hybrids, among the twelve signs.

items.prompt: You want to spot the Moon and the brightest planets. Which band of sky should you scan?

options.label: A belt around the northern pole star only
A belt centered on the celestial equator
A belt about 60° wide along the Milky Way
A belt about 8° either side of the Sun's yearly path

items.explain: The Moon and the brightest planets appear within the zodiac belt, which extends about 8° north and south of the ecliptic.

items.prompt: Long ago the March equinox lay in Aries, but today it lies elsewhere. What caused the shift?

options.label: The slow shift called the precession of the equinoxes
A change in the length of the year
The Sun moving to a new path among the stars
The Moon's orbit tilting over the centuries

items.explain: Due to the precession of the equinoxes, the March equinox point has moved from Aries into Pisces.

items.prompt: Babylonian astronomers split the ecliptic into 12 equal signs. What did they base this on?

options.label: The 12 brightest stars along the ecliptic
The 12 planets they knew of
Twelve schematic months of 30 days each
The 12 hours in a Babylonian night

items.explain: Around the end of the fifth century BC they divided the ecliptic into 12 equal signs by analogy to 12 schematic months of 30 days.

items.prompt: Modern astrologers begin Aries at the March equinox. How did Babylonian astronomers fix their zodiac?

options.label: In relation to the March equinox, as astrologers do
In relation to stars, such as one in Gemini and one in Capricornus
In relation to the Moon's position at each new year
In relation to the day length at each month's start

items.explain: Babylonian astronomers fixed the zodiac in relation to stars, placing the beginning of Cancer at the Rear Twin Star and Aquarius at the Rear Star of the Goat-Fish.

items.prompt: Giving each sign 30° of celestial longitude along the ecliptic created what, according to the sources?

options.label: The first known celestial coordinate system
The first known calendar of 365 days
The first known catalogue of every star
The first known map of Earth's seas

items.explain: Each sign contained 30° of celestial longitude, creating the first known celestial coordinate system.

paragraphs.heading: A belt across the sky
paragraphs.text: The zodiac is a band of sky that runs about 8° on each side of the ecliptic. The ecliptic is the path the Sun appears to trace across the sky over a year. The Moon and the brightest planets also travel within this band.

paragraphs.heading: Twelve signs
paragraphs.text: The band is cut along the ecliptic into 12 equal pieces called signs, each spanning 30°. They roughly match twelve constellations, running from Aries, Taurus and Gemini round to Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces. The word comes from Greek meaning "of or relating to little animals", a name that reflects how many signs are animals or mythical hybrids. People once used the signs to tell the time of year by noting which sign the Sun was in.

paragraphs.heading: Born in Babylon
paragraphs.text: The system, along with measuring angles in 360 degrees, began in Babylonian astronomy in the 1st millennium BC. Near the end of the fifth century BC, Babylonian astronomers split the ecliptic into 12 equal signs, by analogy with 12 idealised months of 30 days. Modern calculations place this between 409 and 398 BC, probably within a few years of 401 BC. Giving each sign 30° created the first known celestial coordinate system.

paragraphs.heading: Fixed to the stars
paragraphs.text: The Babylonians tied the zodiac to particular stars. They began Cancer at the "Rear Twin Star" and Aquarius at the "Rear Star of the Goat-Fish". Modern astrologers, by contrast, start Aries where the Sun sits at the March equinox. To place a planet, Babylonian observers compared it with "normal stars" lying within about 9° of the ecliptic, and their diaries usually gave its position by sign alone.

paragraphs.heading: Travels and drift
paragraphs.text: The idea reached Greek astronomy by the 2nd century BC and also shaped the Hindu zodiac. Ptolemy described how the zodiac is built in the Almagest, his large work of the 2nd century AD. Because of an effect called the precession of the equinoxes, the time of year when the Sun is in a given constellation has shifted since Babylonian times. The March equinox point, once in Aries, has moved into Pisces.

paragraphs.heading: Still in use
paragraphs.text: Astronomers today still use the zodiac's frame, the ecliptic coordinate system, to track objects in the Solar System. It measures latitude from the ecliptic and longitude from the Sun's position at the vernal equinox. Even so, the word zodiac and the names of the twelve signs are now mostly linked with horoscopes and astrology.
